You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test case is testing the Line.revert() method, which is supposed to return a reversed direction line. The test expects the line's direction vector to be negated exactly as produced by Vector3D.negate().

The implementation of Line.revert() currently creates a new Line from the point zero and zero.subtract(direction). The zero and direction fields are presumably Vector3D fields on the line. This approach relies on the subtract method from zero and direction to get the reversed direction but does not use the negate() method of Vector3D directly.

From the Line.reset() method, we see how direction and zero are assigned. The direction is instantiated from delta normalized (delta being p2-p1). The zero vector is computed based on a linear combination involving p1 and delta.

The comment in the bug report mentions that c0.m0() (likely the revert method) only maintains about 10 digits of precision for the direction vector. This loss of precision is important especially when the line's position is far from the origin (likely meaning zero vector is large, causing precision loss when subtracting direction vector). The current revert() implementation creates a new Line using zero.subtract(direction), which involves subtracting direction from zero, possibly losing precision.

The bug report suggests that a simple fix would be to use Vector3D.negate() to get the reversed direction vector, avoiding precision loss.

Therefore the root cause of the failure is that Line.revert() performs the inversion of the direction vector imprecisely by doing zero.subtract(direction) instead of direction.negate(). This causes direction returned by reverted.getDirection() not to match the expectation from the test case, which calls direction.negate() explicitly.

Additionally, the bug report questions mutability of the Line class, since the Line can be constructed from just two points/vectors, but that is secondary.

In summary, the revert method uses zero.subtract(direction) to reverse the direction vector. The subtraction here can cause floating-point imprecision when zero has large magnitude. Using direction.negate() directly would preserve more precision and match the test expectation.

No other recent bug reports appear relevant.

# Next step
Suggest fixing Line.revert() to create the reversed line using the original zero point and the negated direction vector rather than zero.subtract(direction).
org.apache.commons.math3.geometry.euclidean.threed.Line.revert()
